chunks.text: A data structure is a concrete way to store data in a program, written in a specific language. It implements the operations of an ADT. The same ADT can have several data structures behind it, such as an array-based version and a linked version.

cases.question_text: Is a linked version of a list faster than an array-based version?
cases.answer_text: The lesson chunks do not compare the speed of the two versions. They say that the same ADT can have several data structures behind it, such as an array-based version and a linked version.
cases.note: Saying the chunks do not cover it is not a claim; the other sentence is supported. (Edge: a sentence about what the chunks do not cover, plus one supported claim)

chunks.text: Encapsulation puts an object's data and the methods that use that data together in one class, and keeps the data from being changed directly from outside. In Java the fields are usually declared private, and other code works with the object through public methods.

cases.answer_text: Encapsulation keeps an object's data from being changed directly from outside, so the fields are declared private and other code uses public methods. Private fields also make the program run faster.
cases.note: Added unsupported claim. (Edge: one added sentence)
unsupported: Private fields also make the program run faster.

chunks.text: A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.

cases.question_text: Which collection should I use to store unique student IDs?
cases.answer_text: A set does not allow duplicates, so a set is a good fit for storing unique student IDs.
cases.note: The chunk states a set does not allow duplicates; the recommendation follows directly. (Edge: a supported fact plus a recommendation drawn from it)

chunks.text: A getter is a public method that returns the value of a private field. A setter is a public method that changes a field, and it can check the new value first, for example rejecting a negative price.

cases.question_text: For lab 1, what should the setPrice method look like?
cases.answer_text: A setter can check the new value first. For lab 1: public void setPrice(double price) { if (price < 0) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price"); } this.price = price; }
cases.note: Concept supported, but gives finished code for graded lab work. (Edge: concept supported, but finished code for graded work)
